# Behavior Design

*Make the Better Action Easier*

[]{#behavior-design-make-the-better-action-easier}

::: {#chapter-39-start .chapter-epigraph}
> “For a target behavior to happen, a person must have sufficient motivation, sufficient ability, and an effective trigger.”
>
> — B. J. Fogg, [“A Behavior Model for Persuasive Design”](https://doi.org/10.1145/1541948.1541999), 2009, p. 2
:::

Imagine a student who sincerely intends to study before opening email. Each morning the laptop opens onto the inbox, the phone sits beside the keyboard, the first study task is vague, and every message offers a small unit of completion. “Care more” is not yet a design. The current environment contains a prompt, an easy action, and immediate feedback—for email.

The redesign gives the better behavior the same structural advantages. The laptop opens to the problem set. The first task is already written. The phone begins in another room. “After I place my coffee on the desk, I will solve the first visible question before opening email.” A checkmark makes the start visible. The desired action no longer has to defeat a complete competing system.

Behavior design is prescriptive; habit science is descriptive. Explaining a loop does not tell us whether the right response is training, cue removal, substitution, social support, treatment, a new workflow, or structural change. Design begins only after the target and competing behavior are observed precisely.

::: {.callout-note .core-idea icon=false}
## Core Idea

Begin with an action someone wants to take and a specific occasion when it fails to happen. Find what makes starting or continuing difficult, change that condition, and observe the result. A useful design also explains how to resume after a lapse and when to reconsider the goal or seek more support.
:::

![A practical workflow defines an action, finds an obstacle, changes one condition, and tests the result. Review can change the diagnosis; after a lapse or harm, recovery or support may also change the goal or design.](../figures/behavior-design.svg){#fig-behavior-design fig-alt="A vertical five-step workflow moves from defining an action through diagnosis, a changed condition, measurement, and review. A return arrow sends results back to diagnosis; a note addresses recovery and support after a lapse or harm." .phone-fit}

## Learning goals

- Apply one five-step workflow: define the behavior, diagnose the bottleneck, redesign the decisive point, measure, and review.
- Use a diagnostic or planning framework only when it clarifies a specific bottleneck.
- Test whether one small redesign improves an endorsed outcome while protecting agency and recovery.

The [habit chapter](21-habits-wanting-and-self-control.qmd#chapter-21-start) explained how recurring contexts can bring a practiced response to mind. Behavior change becomes difficult when those cues, immediate consequences, and environmental constraints favor the existing behavior (Wood & Rünger, 2016). A useful toolkit begins with diagnosis.

## One primary workflow

The student’s intention is clear, but that does not yet identify the right intervention. A reminder targets forgetting, while the inbox may be winning through a clearer, easier first action. A smaller task addresses effort, but it cannot supply unavailable materials. To spend effort on the condition that actually blocks action, use the same five-step record for personal and organizational behavior:

| Step | Required output | Governing question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Define the behavior** | One observable target action, the competing action, and the situation in which one displaces the other | What would a camera or reliable record show? |
| **2. Diagnose the bottleneck** | The cue, immediate function or consequence, and the main constraint on the target action | Why does the current response win at this moment? |
| **3. Redesign the decisive point** | One change to the cue, action size, friction, prompt, support, or immediate feedback | What is the smallest change that directly addresses the diagnosed bottleneck? |
| **4. Measure** | Baseline, one process signal, one outcome signal, a prediction, and a time-bounded test | What observable pattern would show that the diagnosis was useful? |
| **5. Review** | A review date and a keep, revise, or stop rule, including recovery after a lapse or harm | What will change next if the prediction succeeds or fails? |
: A minimum behavior-design record {#tbl-behavior-design-workflow}

Use this record to connect each change with a diagnosis, returning to earlier steps when new information changes the picture. B=MAP and COM-B can sharpen diagnosis; implementation intentions, WOOP, friction changes, temptation bundling, and precommitment can support a selected redesign.

::: {.callout-note .research-lens icon=false collapse=true}
## Research note: the ideas behind the workflow

@fig-behavior-design brings together several ideas. The Fogg Behavior Model describes motivation, ability, and a cue for action converging at a behavioral moment; its earlier term “trigger” became “prompt” in later presentations (Fogg, 2009, 2020). COM-B treats capability, opportunity, and motivation as interacting conditions, with feedback from behavior (Michie et al., 2011). Research on implementation intentions, habits, and behavior-change maintenance supports planning, feedback, and preparation for obstacles (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006; Kwasnicka et al., 2016; Wood & Rünger, 2016). A lapse or harm may reveal a cue, constraint, support need, or goal that needs reconsideration.

:::

## Optional lens: diagnose the moment with B=MAP {#diagnose-the-moment-with-bmap}

At the intended starting moment, a willing student may still lack a feasible first task, while an easy task may never be noticed. Calling both failures “low motivation” sends the redesign toward the wrong problem. The Fogg Behavior Model offers one moment-level lens: behavior happens when motivation, ability, and a prompt converge (Fogg, 2009, 2020). Use it when Step 2 suggests that a behavior repeatedly fails at a particular moment and it is unclear whether willingness, feasibility, or the prompt is missing. For a desired repeated behavior whose motivation is volatile, making action easier can be more reliable than trying to keep motivation permanently high. Motivation often fluctuates; ability and prompts can sometimes be redesigned.

::: {.callout-note .research-lens icon=false}
## Research Lens: COM-B widens the diagnosis

COM-B asks whether **capability**, **opportunity**, and **motivation** converge (Michie et al., 2011). Capability includes skill, knowledge, energy, and physical ability. Opportunity includes time, tools, permission, safety, and social context. Motivation includes reflective and automatic processes. A motivational speech cannot fix a broken opportunity structure. COM-B is useful when B=MAP's moment-level diagnosis needs a broader account of resources and institutions.

| Diagnostic lens | Question | Inspect before prescribing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capability | Can the person perform it? | Knowledge, skill, memory, physical capacity, emotional regulation |
| Opportunity | Does the environment allow and support it? | Time, access, tools, permission, safety, norms |
| Motivation | Do reflective and automatic motives point toward it? | Values, incentives, emotion, identity, habit, anticipated reward |
| Prompt | What calls for action at the right moment? | Reminder, event, place, internal state, anchor routine |
| Ability now | Is the action feasible in this real moment? | Time, effort, money, complexity, social risk, disruption |
: COM-B and B=MAP as complementary diagnostic lenses {#tbl-21-diagnosis}

Use these questions to identify when the barrier calls for resources, access, treatment, or organizational change.
:::

## Tiny is strategic

Old behavior is practiced, cued, familiar, and usually rewarded now. A new behavior is uncertain and its benefit may arrive later. The first action should therefore be small enough to survive an ordinary low-motivation day: open the manuscript; put on the shoes; write one question; take one breath before responding. Tiny is not the destination. It is an entry point that lowers friction, reduces threat, creates data, and can grow after it begins.

Fogg's practical recipe is: **After I [reliable anchor], I will [tiny behavior]. Then I will [authentically acknowledge completion].** The anchor supplies a prompt; the tiny action lowers the ability threshold; acknowledgment makes progress detectable. Test the recipe by observing the cue, feasibility, feedback, and repetition.

Motivation arrives in waves. A workshop, health result, deadline, or inspiring idea may make an ambitious plan feel easy. The plan then has to run on a tired Wednesday. Use high motivation for setup—schedule the class, prepare the tools, remove the app, arrange the partner, automate the transfer, write the first prompt—rather than as fuel the routine must consume every day.

## Optional tools for a diagnosed bottleneck

Choose a tool only after the workflow has identified what prevents the target action. A goal that is clear but not retrieved at the critical moment may need a cue-linked plan. An action that is too difficult may need a smaller start or less friction. A delayed benefit may need immediate feedback or a carefully chosen reward. Predictable future temptation may justify precommitment.

Implementation intentions link an anticipated situation to a specified response, helping a goal be retrieved and acted on at the relevant moment (Gollwitzer, 1999). Instead of saying "I will study more," a student says: "If I finish breakfast on weekdays, then I study for twenty-five minutes before email." Instead of "I will be less defensive," a manager says: "If I receive criticism, then I ask one clarifying question before explaining." Instead of "I will save money," a person says: "If I receive my salary, then I transfer 10 percent to savings immediately." A complete plan makes the **if/then, where, when, and how** recoverable at the critical moment. In a workplace vaccination study, a reminder asking employees to write the date and time of their planned visit increased vaccination compared with a reminder without that planning field, illustrating how a valued intention can fail until it is attached to a concrete execution opportunity (Milkman et al., 2011).

WOOP adds a useful self-regulation bridge: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan. The person identifies a feasible and meaningful wish, imagines the valued outcome, identifies the real internal or contextual obstacle, and forms an if-then plan. The exercise connects a valued future with an anticipated obstacle, rather than assuming that imagining success will make action follow. Evidence on mental contrasting with implementation intentions supports modest average gains in goal attainment relative to control conditions without the combined exercise, with variation across goals and settings (Oettingen, 2012; Wang et al., 2021).

Friction is a behavioral force. When friction is an important diagnosed bottleneck, reducing it can support a desired behavior; adding proportionate friction can interrupt an unwanted one. Keep the book visible and the phone away. Remove saved payment information. Put exercise clothes by the bed. Create a meeting template. Make near-miss reporting simple and nonpunitive. Require a decision question before scheduling a meeting. Many behaviors live near the margin, so small barriers or small reductions in effort can matter.

Defaults change what happens when no active choice is made, so they belong to the choice path rather than to this moment-level behavior diagnosis. [Chapter 40](40-choice-architecture-the-environment-gets-a-vote.qmd#set-the-starting-point-defaults-and-active-choice) examines their mechanisms, boundary conditions, and ethics. Here, keep the intervention local: change the effort required to perform the target or competing action without treating non-response as informed preference.

Temptation bundling attaches an immediate reward to a beneficial behavior whose benefits are delayed. In a field experiment, making tempting audiobooks available only at the gym initially increased visits compared with a control group given a bookstore gift certificate and encouragement to exercise (Milkman et al., 2014). A person might likewise reserve a favorite podcast for walking or special coffee for difficult reading. The bundle works best when the reward is exclusive enough to pull the desired behavior and does not sabotage the goal. It can be fragile when routines are disrupted or the tempting activity becomes available elsewhere.

Precommitment protects future behavior from predictable future states (Thaler & Shefrin, 1981). Examples include app blockers, cancellation penalties, and restricted-access accounts, with different degrees of reversibility and enforcement. The [intertemporal-choice chapter](19-intertemporal-decision-making-why-later-loses-to-now.qmd#chapter-19-start) distinguishes commitment evidence from the retracted deadline study; an appealing example cannot establish that a device works. A good commitment device preserves dignity and allows recovery after failure. A bad one creates shame without changing the loop.

## Design an attention boundary

External systems compete for the same cue and action. Notifications, autoplay, badges, saved payment, infinite feeds, and social feedback reduce the effort required to enter their loops. Ward and colleagues (2017) reported lower cognitive performance when participants’ own phones were nearby. A later meta-analysis found limited support for a smaller, narrower effect: pooled impairment appeared for working memory, while other cognitive outcomes showed no significant effect (Parry, 2024). This differs from an actual notification interrupting a task, discussed in [Attention](03-attention-what-becomes-evidence.qmd#designed-attention). Diagnose the interruption or checking pattern you can observe rather than assuming that every nearby phone drains capacity. When attention switches away from an unfinished task, part of the previous task can remain mentally active—**attention residue**—and reduce performance on the next task (Leroy, 2009).

A boundary makes the intended action easier to continue and the competing loop less available. It may be a device location, notification rule, website block, timebox, saved stopping point, shutdown ritual, or agreement with another person. The design question is not “How do I resist every interruption?” It is “Which boundary keeps the intended task from being asked to win the same contest repeatedly?”

Digital engagement also needs an audit:

| Loop feature | Helpful use | Capture risk | Agency safeguard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Trigger | Timely medication or coordination prompt | Continuous interruption and anxiety cue | User-controlled timing and batching |
| Easy action | Removes needless access friction | One-tap entry into an endless loop | Visible stopping point and deliberate continuation |
| Variable feedback | Makes practice interesting | Repeated checking for uncertain social reward | Bounded sessions and honest expectations |
| Investment | Saves progress or supports relationships | Sunk data and streaks make exit painful | Portability, pause, easy cancellation |
| Measurement | Tracks a learner's endorsed outcome | Optimizes clicks or time while welfare falls | Measure goal attainment, well-being, and opportunity cost |
: A humane digital-loop audit {#tbl-21-digital-loop}

The ethical issue is whether a system exploits uncertainty, social anxiety, or craving against the user's interests and whether stopping remains practicable.

## Organizational habits

An employee can intend to speak openly while a meeting repeatedly makes silence the safer response. Improving that person’s habit alone leaves the other participants’ reactions and the reporting rules in place. An organizational **routine** involves several people, roles, tools, and rules; changing it requires tracing how their actions sustain the pattern. Deliberate incentives and formal requirements can maintain it alongside automatic responses.

A meeting that rewards confident updates and makes bad news costly can repeatedly hide useful information. Calling for openness changes little if the first person to reveal a problem is punished. Apply the workflow to an observable interaction: who does what, what follows immediately, and which part of the process could support a better response?



## Mini-case: the defensive meeting loop

A product team says it wants psychological safety and better decisions. Yet every Monday meeting follows the same pattern. A project lead presents progress. A senior manager asks a skeptical question. The project lead hears the question as criticism and begins explaining why the team made reasonable choices. Other members go quiet. The manager interprets the defensiveness as lack of ownership and asks more pointed questions. The project lead becomes more defensive. The meeting ends with action items but little learning.

Nobody intended to create this pattern. The senior manager intended to improve the project. The project lead intended to protect the team. Other members intended to avoid conflict. But together they created a routine.

The episode suggests a loop to investigate: a skeptical question cues a defensive reply, while explaining protects the project lead’s standing in the moment. Ask participants what they understood and inspect repeated interactions to distinguish this explanation from a misunderstanding or missing context.

Begin with one change: before questioning the update, the manager asks, “What would be most useful for us to challenge?” Keep the rest of the meeting reasonably stable during this small test and record whether a concrete uncertainty is raised before a defensive exchange begins. If the question helps, a later test might add the project lead’s plan: “If I hear criticism, I will ask which risk the question is meant to clarify.” Introducing both changes together would make their separate contributions harder to learn.

The revised procedure gives participants another response to practice. As [Chapter 28](28-authority-groupthink-and-shared-responsibility.qmd#match-the-safeguard-to-the-missing-step) emphasized, the manager’s subsequent conduct still matters: inviting a concern and punishing the answer would teach silence again. Track whether concerns appear earlier and receive useful responses, including concerns that challenge the manager’s own view.

This case illustrates the deepest practical lesson of habit science: do not rely on the self you hope will appear in the moment. Design for the self and the team that will actually be there.

## Habit design is power

Changing cues, effort, and consequences changes what other people are likely to do. The student can endorse a study arrangement for himself; a platform designer or manager must also consider whose goals the arrangement serves.

Ask whether users can understand the design, choose otherwise, and discover its costs. A streak may encourage practice while making rest feel like failure; a reporting dashboard may improve coordination while exposing staff to surveillance. Measure the outcome people value, alongside any burden or loss of control.



## Fresh starts, identity, and social context

A new semester can make a fresh study plan feel credible, while the same inbox and vague first task can still win on the first morning. To make the transition useful, identify which conditions will actually change. Stable contexts help cues retrieve practiced responses. Moving, changing jobs, or altering a recurring schedule can disrupt the cues that normally retrieve a response without necessarily erasing what was learned. A temporal landmark can also create a psychological “fresh start” (Dai et al., 2014). A transition may therefore be a useful occasion to prepare a new starting routine, with the new routine ready to practice.

But contexts are not only physical. They are also social and identity-based. People repeat behaviors partly because those behaviors answer the question: What do people like us do, and who am I becoming when I do this? Identity-based motivation can make difficulty mean “this matters to people like me” or “this proves I do not belong” (Oyserman, 2009). Use identity as a flexible hypothesis—“I am becoming someone who asks one question before defending”—not a purity test. A rigid identity can turn rest into failure, a lapse into shame, and revision into betrayal.

## Relapse, recovery, and ethics

Many behavior-change attempts include lapses, especially when old cues remain strong or circumstances change. A lapse supplies an occasion to examine which cue, state, reward, friction, social pressure, or obstacle was underestimated. When lapses are plausible, a good design specifies a recovery path before one occurs.

Recovery begins with diagnosis: What cue appeared? What state was the person in? What immediate function did the old action serve? Was the desired action too difficult, poorly prompted, socially unsafe, or no longer worth pursuing? Restart at the next workable cue and review the support needed. Repeated lapses can show that the environment, support, goal, or treatment needs to change.

Recovery from addiction may require clinical assessment and evidence-based treatment alongside changes to everyday routines (Volkow et al., 2016).[^ch39-addiction-care]

::: {.callout-caution .evidence-and-boundary-conditions icon=false}
## Willpower is not one depletable fuel

The classic ego-depletion account of willpower as a depletable resource has faced serious replication and measurement challenges (Hagger et al., 2016). Fatigue, motivation, beliefs, opportunity costs, and context offer alternative explanations of changes in self-control. [Appendix F](../appendices/appendix-f-when-evidence-breaks.qmd#direct-or-coordinated-tests-that-did-not-reproduce-the-focal-result) tracks the disputed evidence and its boundaries.
:::

## Measure the loop, not the story

A learning app can increase check-ins while weakening deep learning; a negotiation script can be used frequently while eliciting no new information. The redesign appears to be working because activity rose, yet the intended outcome may be no better. Measurement must distinguish performing the new routine from achieving its purpose. Record a baseline before intervention: the observable target and competing behavior, contexts, delay, and immediate consequence. Then choose the few signals that would show whether the diagnosis was right:

- **Behavior:** Did the observable action change?
- **Process:** Did the cue, tiny start, question, or pause occur?
- **Outcome:** Did learning, health, judgment, cooperation, or well-being improve?
- **Maintenance:** Does change persist after novelty and intensive support decline?
- **Equity and access:** Who can use the design, and who bears new friction?
- **Unintended effects:** What useful behavior, trust, autonomy, rest, or flexibility was displaced?

Use the smallest credible reversible test: target, baseline, prediction, intervention, measure, review date, and stop or revision rule.

| Tool | Best used when... | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Implementation intention | The goal is clear but follow-through fails at the critical moment. | If I feel the urge to explain during feedback, then I ask one clarifying question first. |
| WOOP | Positive intention needs an honest obstacle and a concrete plan. | Wish: prepare earlier. Outcome: calm negotiation. Obstacle: vague starting point. Plan: if unclear, then write three interests. |
| Friction design | The behavior is sensitive to small barriers or ease. | Phone outside bedroom; saved card removed; document opened before leaving work. |
| Temptation bundling | The desired behavior has delayed benefits and needs immediate reward. | Only listen to a favorite audiobook while walking. |
| Precommitment | Future states predictably defeat current intentions. | Automatic savings, scheduled class, app blocker, accountability partner. |
| Context change | Old cues keep recruiting the old behavior. | Use a new study location, new commute, new meeting script, or new semester routine. |
| BRAIN observation prompts | A mild everyday impulse is present and a pause may help choice. | Use Chapter 21’s classroom mnemonic to notice the impulse and pause before acting. |
| Relapse plan | A missed repetition could become identity proof. | If I miss once, then I restart at the next cue with the smallest version. |
: Behavior-change tools and their best uses {#tbl-21-1}

## Practice Lab: behavior-design studio

Choose one mild, real behavior and complete the one-page record in @tbl-behavior-design-workflow:

1. **Define:** write the observable target, competing action, and recurring situation.
2. **Diagnose:** name the cue, the current action's immediate function, and the single most important bottleneck. Use B=MAP or COM-B only if it improves this diagnosis.
3. **Redesign:** change one decisive point. Choose no more than one primary tool from @tbl-21-1 and state exactly what will be different in the environment or response.
4. **Measure:** record a baseline, one process signal, one outcome signal, and a directional prediction for a short reversible test.
5. **Review:** set a date and write the rule for keeping, revising, or stopping the design. Add one recovery action after a lapse and one harm or displaced value that would trigger reconsideration.

Conclude with one sentence: “If this diagnosis is useful, the mechanism should be visible as…” The completed record—not the number of frameworks used—is the output.

## Take it forward


Choose a recurring moment when an intention loses to the easier response. Make one feasible change to that moment, observe what happens, and use the result to revise your diagnosis. A plan becomes more useful when it includes a way to resume after a lapse.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Optional Media Lab

Before viewing, predict what evidence would distinguish pleasure from prediction error or motivation from ability. After viewing, identify one defensible claim, one overclaim to avoid, and one behavior-design transfer.
